articles.title: Los expertos coinciden: el salario mínimo debería subir 60 euros al mes en 2027, hasta los 1.281 euros
articles.standfirst: A esta conclusión ha llegado el grupo anexo al Ministerio de Trabajo
articles.summary: A esta conclusión ha llegado el grupo anexo al Ministerio de Trabajo
articles.body: Mientras los diferentes partidos políticos se encuentran en plena campaña electora, el Ministerio de Trabajo sigue trabajando para llegar a un acuerdo para una nueva subida del salario mínimo. La cartera dirigida por Yolanda Díaz ha mantenido nuevas conversaciones con el comité de expertos anexo a su Ministerio. Estos han llegado a la conclusión de que el salario mínimo debería subir 60 euros al mes en 2027. O lo que es lo mismo, a partir del próximo año debería situarse en 1.281 euros. La intención de Yolanda Díaz es que la próxima subida cubra parte del poder adquisitivo que se ha perdido con el paso de los años por la inflación. Ahora mismo, la cuantía que se recibe es de 1.221 euros. Del mismo modo, se recuerda que quien tenga el salario mínimo, tampoco deberá pagar el impuesto sobre la renta (IRPF) con esta subida, como ya se ha hecho en años anteriores. Esta subida del 4,9% dista sobre lo pedido por los sindicatos, quienes querían fijar la subida en un 7%. Caso opuesto al de la patronal, que rechazó un nuevo incremento del salario. Lo cierto es que el Gobierno puede consultar ambas opiniones, pero no es necesario tenerlas en cuenta a la hora de fijar una subida. Es el Ejecutivo quien tiene la potestad absoluta para fijar la cuantía del salario mínimo en el Estatuto de los Trabajadores. En este caso, ni la patronal ni los sindicatos están completamente de acuerdo con la subida que se pretende aplicar. La intención de Yolanda Díaz es que la nueva cuantía del salario mínimo quede aprobada antes de las elecciones generales del 29N. Algo que Antonio Garamendi, presidente de CEOE, ha descrito como “una estrategia exclusivamente de campaña política".

articles.title: Why did America swing back to the Democrats? It was the economy all along
articles.summary: President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress were elected to fix the economy. Now Americans feel even worse about it than they did two years ago.
articles.body: At face value, it’s not all that complicated. President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress were elected in November 2024 to fix the economy. Now it’s November 2026, and Americans feel even worse about it than they did two years ago. So, it’s the economy, stupid. But with respect to James Carville, it’s not quite that simple. America’s economy is in surprisingly good shape. Unemployment is low – low enough for economists to consider the US economy to be at “full employment.” Overall consumer spending, the bedrock of America’s economy, has remained mostly resilient. And the AI revolution has revved an economic engine so powerful it’s projected to become the largest spending boom in modern US history. If the economy is so strong, what got Americans fed up with Republicans just two years after they voted them into power? Inflation is back, and voters drew a straight line connecting Trump’s signature policies to their financial anxieties. Tariffs. Lax AI regulation. Strict immigration restrictions. And especially the Iran war. “If it weren’t for the war in Iran, this would be a very different midterm election,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. The cost of living Americans still haven’t adjusted to the significant jump in the price of … well, pretty much everything … since 2021. Inflation had come back down to earth in the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency, but that wasn’t enough to convince voters to give Democrats another chance in 2024. And that anger about the high cost of living has festered throughout Trump’s return to office. Still, Trump and Republicans had a fairly compelling economic story to tell in the early part of this year. Then America went to war with Iran, and everything changed. Oil prices surged to four-year highs. Diesel prices hit a record. And gas prices had never been this expensive on an Election Day. Americans may hate inflation, but they get particularly irate about high fuel prices. Gas prices are plastered on giant billboards all over town, and filling a tank serves as a weekly reminder about how much more they’re shelling out: High gas and diesel prices alone have added $1,150 in costs for the average US household since the start of the war, according to Brown University researchers. As fuel prices rose, bond yields surged, and so too did mortgage rates – recently rising at their fastest pace in three years. After three straight years of paycheck gains outpacing price hikes, that trend kicked into reverse in March. Rebounding inflation has been eating into workers’ take-home pay ever since – and the average American’s real pay has shrunk since Trump has been back in office. Americans blame Trump It’s not a surprise that Americans had fond memories of the economy under Trump’s first term. At every point during Trump 1.0, Americans’ hard-earned dollars stretched further than prices – their pay gains nearly doubled the pace of inflation throughout his first four years in office. That’s why Americans polled by CNN in October 2024 favored Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris as a better custodian of the economy by 15 percentage points. No shock there: Biden’s net approval on the economy was -31 points in the final CNN poll taken before he dropped out of the race. Trump’s marks are now worse than Biden’s. By a wide margin: His net approval on the economy is -46 points, according to an October CNN poll. Trump 2.0 has been a completely different story than Trump 1.0. For many Americans, it seems like costs are spiraling out of control and the American Dream is unattainable. The Trump administration and congressional Republicans have laid blame at Democrats’ feet for the poor state of financial affairs they inherited. But some of Trump’s policies – especially his unpopular war – clearly made Americans’ cost of living worse. It’s not just gas prices, which have added about $75 a month to people’s expenses. It’s other costs that voters associate with Trump and the Republicans – some of which are adding hundreds of dollars a month to their bills. For example: “Let’s say, for the sake of argument Biden totally screwed up: That in no way exonerates Trump,” said Steven Durlauf, an economist at the University of Chicago who researches wealth inequality and mobility. “Inflation has been badly managed by Trump. Voters have to place responsibility with the administration’s policies.” All the evidence points to the voters doing just that. That’s a big reason why Trump’s Republican party took a beating in Tuesday’s midterm election. Out of options Inflation is only part of the story. Many Americans feel like the economy has left them behind. The K-shaped economy accounts for some of that: Wealthier Americans with money in the stock market and who own a home are significantly more immune to rising costs than less-affluent Americans who are increasingly living paycheck to paycheck. A big part of the problem is the lack of available options to achieve the American Dream: A massive undersupply of childcare options and housing have priced out many folks and have denied access for some who can. “The middle-class ideal is becoming increasingly unobtainable,” said Durlauf. The same is becoming true of the job market. Although still relatively strong, jobs are by no means booming like they had been in the immediate post-pandemic years. Mass layoffs haven’t become the norm, but for folks without a job, applications feel like they’re going into the ether. “Another way to say low-hire, low-fire job market is lack-of-opportunity job market,” Long said. In this economy, many Americans just feel stuck.

articles.title: Democrats won control of Congress. Their economic agenda is set to target healthcare, tariffs, and Trump's allies.
articles.summary: Democrats won majorities in both houses of Congress on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Democrats retook power in Washington on Tuesday, flipping key House and Senate seats to command majorities in both chambers of Congress.

The power shift creates a new platform for Democrats to launch investigations of President Trump's economic allies — Elon Musk, to name one — and pass bills that may be unlikely to become law but will mark a sharp change in the political climate for business leaders and economic issues after two years of unified Republican control.

The change also appears set to elevate figures like Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and others to prominent positions with oversight over economic policy.

Democrats are planning "a shock-and-awe legislative sprint," the New York Times reported , on issues like healthcare subsidies and Trump's tariffs, which could prompt a wave of bills to pass the House but stall against the 60-vote threshold in the Senate. Even in the minority, Senate rules mean Republicans retain the power to stop legislation.

Democrats are also likely to seek areas of bipartisan agreement on pharmaceuticals, the housing market, and AI data centers, all sectors that both Republicans and Democrats have spotlighted on the campaign trail.

Divided government, of course, may also set the stage for political clashes that could destabilize markets and the broader economy.

"While conventional wisdom suggests equities tend to rally following midterm elections, particularly when the outcome produces divided government, we caution that the post-election environment may look considerably different this cycle," Raymond James Washington Policy Analyst Ed Mills warned in a pre-election note.

He added that much of the recent volatility has been driven by unexpected moves from the White House. "We believe Trump will increasingly test the limits of executive authority during the remainder of his term," Mills wrote.

'Lawyer up': An expected focus on Elon Musk and Trump's economic team

The House is set to be led by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who has been notably tight-lipped about his plans .

He met with Democratic volunteers as Election Day wound down and told reporters , "We're relentlessly focused on driving down the high cost of living and fighting for an affordable America."

Jeffries avoided the question of whether he would reach out to Trump, while the president told the New York Times he will accept the election results .

Going by early signals, Democrats intend to aim their new powers at an array of high-profile targets, with Musk chief among them, as part of a far-reaching effort to impose new checks on the Trump administration.

articles.body:
The campaign ads are gone from my television, and I’m grateful. The price tag is harder to forget.

OpenSecrets projected the 2026 midterms at $11.9 billion , which would be a record for any midterm. That is more than four times the $2.9 billion the EPA announced in May to help states replace lead pipes. We spent a fortune arguing about the cost of living — now the winners have to do something about it.

But Washington has never learned the lesson that a budget is a promise you make to your future self.

Congress returns Nov. 9 for the lame-duck session, and government funding runs out December 11 . In 1761 London, traders who defaulted on their debts were said to waddle out of Exchange Alley like lame ducks . The government has now run a deficit for 25 straight fiscal years . Debt is still the story.

Fiscal 2026 closed this fall with a $1.99 trillion deficit . Interest on the debt topped $1 trillion and now exceeds defense spending — only Social Security and Medicare cost more. Interest alone consumed 19 percent of all federal revenue . And what principal we do theoretically pay each year, we only do it by borrowing more. This is how the national debt has passed $40 trillion . We are effectively paying only the interest on an ever-growing loan, and we’re calling it governing.

It isn’t just Democrats — Republicans like to spend too. The cure for a debt problem is restraint paired with growth. Some of that growth is already arriving. The Bureau of Economic Analysis reports, in preliminary figures, that foreign investors spent $232.2 billion to acquire, establish, or expand U.S. businesses in 2025 , up 49.5 percent from 2024. Manufacturing took $121.8 billion of it, and Japan was the largest source at $50.5 billion . The White House credits President Trump’s agenda for the surge. Economists can debate where the credit belongs, but the money is landing in American manufacturing, which broadens the tax base.

Still, voters have been promised relief on prices by the party whose policies pushed them up. The $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan landed in March 2021, with the economy already in a strong rebound. The San Francisco Fed estimated that it added about 0.3 percentage points to inflation each year through 2022 . Other economists put the effect at 2 to 3 points . Even Biden’s own economists didn’t dispute that it contributed .

I live in California, where one party makes the rules and everyone else pays for them. A 12-cent gas tax increase , signed by Gov. Jerry Brown in 2017, took effect that November. Regulators at the Air Resources Board say the low-carbon fuel standard adds another 8 to 10 cents a gallon. This week, AAA put the California average at $5.94, versus $4.22 nationally . That gap is $1.72 a gallon, and Sacramento’s taxes and mandates are part of it.

Then there’s the $20 fast-food wage, which researchers have found raised restaurant prices 3.3 percent to 3.6 percent in California metro areas relative to others.

Federal border policy lands on local budgets, too. The Congressional Budget Office found that the immigration surge beginning in 2021 cost state and local governments a net $9.2 billion in 2023 , with $19.3 billion in spending against $10.1 billion in taxes paid. More than half of that spending went to schools, shelter, and border security. Each of these costs is a policy choice, and families absorb every one of them.

Thomas Sowell wrote that there are no solutions, only tradeoffs . Congress forgets this every budget cycle. Every dollar funding a program is a dollar collected in taxes, borrowed or printed. The Declaration of Independence says governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed . I never consented to a $1 trillion in annual interest payments. Neither did my sons.

Critics will say that spending cuts hurt the vulnerable. Fair enough, but family that spent 19 percent of its paycheck on interest would call a financial planner. Interest payments buy nothing for anyone, and they crowd out the programs both parties claim to love. The non-partisan Congressional Budget Office projects net interest will reach nearly $2.5 trillion a year by 2036 .

Lame ducks have votes to spare, so here are my suggestions: Pass full-year appropriations at or below this year’s level, with no holiday omnibus stuffed with extras. If Majority Leader John Thune brings a debt limit increase to the floor, attach enforceable spending caps. Require every new program to name its offset before it gets a vote. Households have to live by that rule, and businesses do too. Congress should try it for a change.

Lame ducks still vote — now is the time to take those politically difficult but necessary votes they didn’t want to take before the election. Both parties found $11.9 billion for campaign ads. They can find the will to balance a checkbook. Future generations will inherit the tab, and they are watching how we handle this now.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

articles.title: LemFi unveils its biggest product expansion and new global brand, 'Ambition has no passport'
articles.summary: LemFi, the financial platform for people building lives across borders, announced its new global brand platform, , alongside a completely rebuilt app,
articles.body: LemFi, the financial platform for people building lives across borders, announced its new global brand platform, , alongside a completely rebuilt app, launching the largest product expansion in its history.More than two million customers rely on LemFi to move money to more than 30 countries, with over $2 billion in monthly transaction volume, and the company plans to add more countries next year. The expanded platform, “Ambition has no passport”, brings savings and credit in the UK, eSIMs in more than 150+ destinations, alongside LemFi’s existing international payments service.People who move countries arrive with a career, a qualification and a savings record, only to find that almost none of it counts. A credit history rarely survives a border crossing. Around 304 million people now live outside the country where they were born, sending some $905 billion home each year. Yet many financial services remain designed around individual products or customers living their financial lives in a single country. LemFi is building its platform around that gap, extending from the international transfers on which the company was founded into a wider range of financial services designed for people whose lives span borders.Left: Rian Cochran, Co-founder and CEO of LemFi; right: Ridwan Olalere, Co-founder and CEO of LemFi“We started LemFi because sending money home was broken. What we learned is that the harder problem starts after the transfer,” said Ridwan Olalere, co-founder and CEO of LemFi. “Our customers are building careers and businesses in one country while supporting people in another, and the financial system treats them as if they can only exist in one place at a time. That is the wrong answer for people this ambitious, so we have rebuilt LemFi to work the way their lives do. Ambition travels. The infrastructure behind it should travel too.”Inside LemFi’s expanded platformTransfers, still at the heart of it. Send money to more than 30 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond, from the same account that now saves, borrows and connects.Savings that stay within reach in the UK. The LemFi Instant Access Savings Account currently pays a boosted 5% AER for the first six months from account opening; it then reverts to 3.04% AER (tracker), tracking the Bank of England base rate. Accounts open from £1, with no penalty for withdrawals. Deposits are held by ClearBank and protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor.A credit history that travels in the UK. A revolving credit line, available subject to availability, is issued by Lemfi Credit through Pillar, the FCA-regulated credit provider LemFi acquired in 2025. It is available as a virtual card through Apple Pay and Google Pay and can be used for both spending and sending. Eligible customers can also see their Equifax credit score in the app for free.eSIM in more than 150+ destinations, in every market. Buy mobile data before arriving, with no SIM swap and no roaming bill.A brand and an app rebuilt togetherThe app has been re-architected from the ground up to hold several products across several countries in a single account, rather than bolting them onto a transfer app. The redesign also brings LemFi’s products to the forefront of the experience, making them easier to discover and creating an architecture that lets the company add new services as it expands.LemFi has also introduced its new global brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, reflecting its focus on customers building careers, businesses, families and financial lives across borders. The new identity spans LemFi’s product interface, website, marketing and social channels and will roll out across its global markets.“LemFi started as a way to send money home. Our customers turned it into a way to build a life across borders,” said Isabel Ron-Pedrique, VP of Design and Brand at LemFi. “They are not defined by the country they left. They are defined by what they are building. Ambition has no passport is not a line we placed on top of the product. It is the idea the whole system is built from, from the app you open in the morning to the poster you walk past on the way to work. We have built this brand to keep up with them”Savings and credit are available in the UK at launch, with other markets to follow.Disclaimer - The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.You use AI every day. articles.title: AMD's AI megadeals with OpenAI and Meta just cost it $1.1 billion: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: A record quarter came with a twist for AMD: Its profits now move against its own stock price.
articles.body:
OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) and Meta ( META ) could buy 320 million AMD ( AMD ) shares for a penny apiece. That's $3.2 million for stock worth about $155 billion, and AMD just got its first bill for the deal.

The chipmaker beat Wall Street's estimates on Tuesday, with record data center sales of about $8.5 billion, nearly double a year ago, and a forecast of about $17 billion in fourth quarter revenue. The stock jumped as much as 9% in after-hours trading after closing at $484 before turning lower in premarket trading.

But tucked into the results was a $1.1 billion charge tied to that penny promise, which comes in the form of warrants — contracts that let the holder buy a company's stock at a set price. The charge came to $0.66 per share in the results. Last quarter, that line was zero.

Here's the deal: OpenAI and Meta each agreed to buy AMD chips for data centers drawing up to 6 gigawatts. That's about five DeLoreans' worth of the 1.21 gigawatts Doc Brown needed to time travel in the 1985 movie "Back to the Future."

In return, each can buy up to 160 million shares at a penny. The shares unlock as the chips ship, and the final batch requires AMD's stock to hit $600, according to company filings for OpenAI and Meta . Fully unlocked, the two would own about 16% of the enlarged company, by Yahoo Finance calculations. The Motley Fool ran the share-count math in October.

So why now? AMD began booking the warrants as it shipped its new MI450 chips, CFO Jean Hu said on Tuesday's call. The charge mostly reflected "the increase in our share price and the changes in the estimated probability of meeting the warrant conditions," she said. The stock rose about 21% last quarter and finished on Sept. 25 at $630, above that $600 line.

And the tab is likely to grow. Hu said she expects the charge "to increase as we and our customers progress under this agreement," with amounts swinging on AMD's stock price. Every rally and every chip shipment can add to it.

It's all on paper, though. The charges "will not affect our non-GAAP results or free cash flow ," Hu said.

AMD is stocking up for a $17 billion quarter

Meanwhile, AMD is loading up for what it expects to be its biggest quarter ever. Inventory jumped about $3 billion to a record $11.5 billion, four times the largest quarterly increase since at least 2009, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from company filings.

That build came at a price. Free cash flow shrank to about $550 million, compared with the nearly $2 billion analysts expected, according to Bloomberg. Debt more than doubled to about $7 billion after an August bond sale.

articles.title: CVS to split into two companies, in major breakup of its $117 billion healthcare empire
articles.summary: CVS Health said Wednesday it is splitting into two companies, marking one of the largest shakeups in the healthcare industry. It’s a major reversal of the mergers that brought together the nation’s largest drugstore retailer along with health insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager Caremark.
articles.body: CVS Health said Wednesday it is splitting into two companies, marking one of the largest shakeups in the healthcare industry. It’s a major reversal of the mergers that brought together the nation’s largest drugstore retailer along with health insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager Caremark. The breakup unwinds a strategy that began in 2007, when CVS merged with Caremark, which handles prescription benefits available to people with health insurance. In 2018, CVS acquired Aetna for $69 billion. “We’re basically taking what I believe is one great company and making it two,” said CVS CEO David Joyner in a statement Wednesday. The company split will have little impact on the way people shop at CVS – the company didn’t announce any closures as part of the news. And it won’t affect what you pay for prescriptions. Pharmacy benefit management businesses work on the backend, negotiating directly with drugmakers on the cost of prescription drugs and thus what customers pay. But CVS’s drugstores and Caremark insurance operate separately. Splitting into two companies won’t change how they function. Shares of CVS Health, which had been up about 15% so far this year, fell 10% in early trading after initially ticking up in premarket trading. Shareholders will get shares of both companies in a tax-free transaction expected to close in early 2028, according to the company. CVS also reported higher third-quarter earnings and revenue Wednesday, due primarily to better results from its Health Care Benefits segment. The company also raised its earnings guidance for the rest of this year. CVS has 9,000 locations across the United States, 800 of which operate “MinuteClinics” staffed by nurse practitioners and physician assistants. It has 30,000 pharmacists and 200,000 employees in its stores, the company said during an earnings call Wednesday.

articles.title: Novo Nordisk CEO: Wegovy pill 'exceeded our expectations'
articles.summary: The Wegovy pill looks like a win for Novo Nordisk.
articles.body:
The Wegovy pill looks like a win for Novo Nordisk ( NVO ) after what some on Wall Street saw as a slower-than-expected consumer uptake.

"The Wegovy pill has exceeded our expectations," Novo Nordisk CEO Mike Doustdar said on Sozzi Unleashed . Doustdar said the pill will be available in 20 countries by next year.

Novo Nordisk continued down its path of delivering better results for investors on Wednesday.

Third quarter sales gained 4% to DKK 79.2 billion ($11.9 billion).

Sales of the new Wegovy pill hauled in DKK 5.4 billion ($811 million). The pill was available in the US, UAE, UK, and Germany and has since expanded to four additional markets.

The company raised its full-year outlook for the second time in three months, driven by strength in the Wegovy pill.

Novo Nordisk sees sales and adjusted operating profits rising as much as 2% this year. In August, the company issued an outlook for sales and profit growth ranging from flat to a 6% decline.

"Overall, given the stronger than expected results with a 8% sales beat and 12% operating profit beat and the upgraded guidance implying c. 3% upgrades to Consensus, we expect the shares to outperform by 3-5% today," JPMorgan analyst Richard Vosser said.

articles.title: Dow jumps by 1,300 points as Democrats take control of Congress
articles.summary: US stocks soared Wednesday as Wall Street digested the resounding Democrat sweep in the midterm elections and mulled what a divided government will mean for President Donald Trump’s policy agenda as well as the AI trade.
articles.body: US stocks soared Wednesday as Wall Street digested the resounding Democrat sweep in the midterm elections and mulled what a divided government will mean for President Donald Trump’s policy agenda as well as the AI trade. The Dow surged 1,307 points, or 2.5%, and was set for its best day since April. The S&P 500 rose 1.5%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite gained 1.7%. Stock futures reversed initial losses and turned higher overnight as investors embraced the certainty offered by the decisive results. Investors also warmed to the prospect of policy gridlock under a divided government, which can curb excess spending and create a more predictable outlook for markets. The VIX, which measures expectations for volatility, sank 16%. “The combination of a large Democratic majority in Congress and President Trump’s statement that he is willing to work with the opposition should act as a break on extreme policy outcomes and bring down risk premia,” George Saravelos, global head of FX research at Deutsche Bank, said in a note. Bond yields fluctuated. Expectations that the election outcome could keep a lid on excessive government borrowing and spending initially bolstered US government bonds, sending yields lower. The dollar weakened against a basket of major currencies. “Divided government has generally made it harder for fiscal stimulus to be passed,” Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note. “So that’s eased concerns on the fiscal trajectory a bit.” It “would significantly constrain Trump’s legislative agenda, particularly on taxes, fiscal stimulus and spending,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at trading platform Saxo, in a note on Wednesday. “But Democrats would not have a free hand to rewrite policy either, because Trump retains veto power.” Meanwhile, investors are also trying to discern what key election results could mean for the outlook for data centers, which are the bedrock of the AI trade that has buoyed US markets. Wall Street analysts had expected a strong performance for Democrats, but the extent of the sweep caught some traders off guard. On Kalshi, odds for Gina Hinojosa to win the Texas governor’s race were pinned at less than 20% for most of the year. The proliferation of AI data centers across different states became a critical issue in many campaigns, and Democrat wins in states like Texas raise questions about whether there will be more moratoriums or restrictions that could slow the data center buildout. While most stocks were higher Wednesday, shares of semiconductor chipmakers and other companies involved in the data center buildout fell. Nvidia fell 1%, while an exchange-traded fund tracking AI infrastructure stocks dropped more than 7%. “While a blue wave could spark volatility in certain sectors, such as tech and AI, given growing public opposition to the buildout of data centers, we believe markets can grind higher regardless of the outcome as investors applaud falling uncertainty,” Justin Buell, chief investment officer at Continuity Group, wrote in a note. Shares of Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX fell 3% and 4%, respectively. Musk has made Texas the home for his companies, and Democrats’ victories in the gubernatorial and senate races are casting uncertainty over his future relationship with the state.

articles.title: Democrats' victories in Texas laid bare voter unease over data centers — and signal new hurdles for the industry
articles.summary: Texas is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers.
articles.body:
A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state's first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies.

Texas is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers and was just one place where deep voter unease over the build-out was on display. Voters across the country passed a series of local ballot measures aimed at restricting construction in the years ahead.

Hinojosa, Texas's first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.

"I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state," she told supporters in her victory speech . "The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get."

Her victory was one of a series of wins for Democrats in Texas. The party is also on track to take control of the Texas House , which would give Hinojosa more power to follow through on restrictions even as the state Senate appears set to remain under Republican control.

"We view the Texas gubernatorial race as particularly important for the next leg of the AI trade," wrote Raymond James's Ed Mills in a pre-election note saying that a strong Democratic showing there "could signal a broader electoral wave while increasing concerns about data center moratoriums and more restrictive AI regulation in the nation's largest planned data center development."

Bank of America called the race "one of the highest impact elections for the entire utility sector."

A race that 'could make a real difference'

Hinojosa made opposition to data center construction a central part of her campaign, charging in one ad that Gov. Greg Abbott "works for" Elon Musk.

She staked out plans for a moratorium on new data center construction, stricter regulations on water and power usage, and an end to tax breaks.

Abbott was seeking his fourth term as governor and said last year he wanted Texas to be the "epicenter of AI development."

More recently, he announced a moratorium of his own and said he would support more stringent requirements on power and water usage. Hinojosa immediately charged that Abbott's new proposals amounted to an "election year pause."

Tobin Marcus of Wolfe Research said Texas "is the one state with enough scale and enough difference between the candidates that it could make a real difference."

articles.title: CVS Health to split in two, separating pharmacy business from insurance
articles.summary: CVS Health will split into two companies, separating retail pharmacy from its insurance and pharmacy-benefit operations in a major unwinding.
articles.body: CVS Health said on Wednesday it will split into two companies, separating retail pharmacy from its insurance and pharmacy-benefit operations in a major unwinding of the healthcare conglomerate it spent years building through acquisitions. The split ​comes amid growing scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators of vertically integrated healthcare companies such as CVS. Years of ‌consolidation across the industry have raised concerns that companies controlling multiple parts of the healthcare supply chain could face conflicts of interest, limit competition and contribute to rising healthcare costs. CVS said the separation of its units was expected to be completed in the first half of 2028. The split would ​mark a significant reversal of the company’s strategy of combining retail pharmacy, health insurance and pharmacy-benefit management under one ​roof. CVS built the conglomerate through a series of acquisitions, including its roughly $78 billion purchase of health ⁠insurer Aetna in 2018. Shares of the company were down more than 10% in early trading Wednesday. Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny attributed the premarket decline partly to ​deal-related uncertainty and broader volatility in healthcare stocks following the midterm elections. Following the split, the healthcare solutions company will be referred to ​as CVS Health in the interim. CVS Health CEO David Joyner will lead the healthcare solutions company, while Group President Prem Shah will become CEO of CVS Pharmacy. “From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer ​engagement, affordability, and care coordination,” said Joyner. Health insurers have grappled with elevated medical costs in recent years as consumers increased their ​use of healthcare services, prompting companies to raise premiums, trim benefits and exit less profitable plans. CVS drugstores have also been grappling with pressures, including competition ‌from Amazon ⁠and a shift toward prescription delivery that has reduced store visits, which traditionally generated additional retail purchases. The challenges underscore the increasingly difficult economics of large US drugstore chains. Faced with similar challenges, rival Walgreens sold its Boots pharmacy business and was acquired by private equity firm Sycamore Partners last year following a prolonged sale process. CVS had also explored options including a potential breakup in 2024, ​Reuters reported at the time, as ​the healthcare giant grappled ⁠with challenges across its businesses. Analysts viewed the potential split positively, saying the timing was favorable as CVS’s Pharmacy and Consumer Wellness business had returned to growth after years of underperformance. “Improving financial results probably helped ​with the timing of the move — better to move from a place of strength than ​a place of ⁠weakness,” said Morningstar analyst Julie Utterback. A separation could also help address regulatory scrutiny of CVS’s vertically integrated model, some analysts noted. Separately, the company reported third-quarter results. Its per-share profit of $2.09 beat analysts’ average estimate of $1.65, per data compiled by LSEG. The company also raised its annual adjusted profit ⁠forecast to ​at least $8.20, but said it was maintaining a cautious view for the remainder ​of the year in light of continued elevated medical cost trends and potential macro headwinds. Upon completion of the separation, CVS Health shareholders will own shares in ​both companies.

articles.title: I bonds now pay 5.51%: What to know before you buy
articles.summary: Series I bonds are gaining popularity among savers. Here's how they work and whether they're right for you.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Government-backed Series I bonds now pay higher interest, 5.51% annual interest through April 30, up from 4.26% — is now the time to lock in?

With everyday costs trending upward, many savers may be looking for ways to inflation-proof their wallets — including their savings.

The latest Consumer Price Index showed prices climbed in September , up 3.7% from a year earlier, with gasoline driving more than half of the increase.

One way to hedge against inflation: explore alternative savings options.

Series I bonds are government-backed savings bonds tied to inflation. Each bond is issued at face value with a 30-year final maturity, consisting of a 20-year original maturity period immediately followed by a 10-year extended maturity period.

The bond's composite rate, or earnings rate, has a two-part structure: a fixed rate and an inflation rate. The fixed rate stays the same for the duration of your bond's term, while the inflation rate can change every six months.

I savings bonds earn interest monthly, and that interest is compounded semiannually.

Another benefit of these bonds is that, while they are subject to federal income tax, they are exempt from state and local income tax. Savers can choose whether to report each year's earnings or report their earnings all at once when they cash out their bond. Additionally, if you choose to use your money for qualified higher education expenses, you may not have to shell out any tax on those earnings.

Series I savings bonds issued between Nov. 1, 2026, and April 30, 2027, are currently offering a composite rate of 5.51%, with a 1.40% fixed rate.

Savers can buy I bonds electronically for as little as $25, up to $10,000 per calendar year, through a TreasuryDirect account .

Series I bonds can be an attractive savings vehicle during periods of rising inflation because the combined rate increases alongside inflation, giving savers a built-in hedge against rising prices.

These bonds are also currently offering yields that are well above national averages for other savings vehicles. The national average rate for a traditional savings account is only 0.38%. Money market accounts and certificates of deposit (CDs) offer slightly higher national average rates at 0.63% for money market accounts and 1.76% for a 12-month CD, but this is still significantly less than the going rate for a Series I bond.

If the inflation rate continues to rise, that could translate to even higher returns for bondholders. In 2022, Series I bonds reached rates as high as 9.62%. Unlike your average savings account or CD, investing in this kind of bond can offset the cost of rising inflation. However, this can be a double-edged sword. Because a portion of the rate is variable and tied to current inflation, the rate can fall significantly — sometimes to near zero — meaning your returns could end up being lower than other investments.

These bonds are not without drawbacks, and it's worth understanding the rules and limitations before committing.

These bonds come with a mandatory lockup period. This means that you cannot redeem an I bond for at least 12 months after the purchase date. If there's a chance you'll need to tap into those funds earlier, I bonds aren't the right fit.

After that holding period is over, you can access your money, but doing so within the first five years of holding your bond would incur a penalty of three months' interest.

There are also purchase limits to keep in mind. You can only buy up to $10,000 in electronic I bonds. Before Jan. 1, 2025, you could purchase an additional $5,000 in paper I bonds with your tax refund for a combined maximum of $15,000 per year, but this option has been phased out.

How do Series I bonds compare to HYSAs, and who should get one?

Series I bonds and HYSAs both offer above-average savings rates, but they differ significantly in terms of features and capabilities. If you're the kind of saver who values liquidity and higher maximum deposits, a high-yield savings account may be the better option. The trade-off is that these accounts can also come with monthly fees, and interest rates are not fixed and can be volatile at times.

Savers who value fixed rates and have longer-term savings goals that won't require access to their money in the immediate term can benefit from the stability of a Series I bond; however, the maximum limit of $10,000 could be a deterrent if you aim to save a lump sum for a more costly financial goal.

Ultimately, both savings options can be beneficial and are certainly worth considering with inflation creeping back up.

articles.title: Stocks rally after Democrats march to midterm victories
articles.summary: Stocks rallied on Wednesday morning, after Democrats snatched back control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up by 1,104 points nearly 30 minutes after the opening bell. The Nasdaq composite and S&P 500 were up by more than 500 and 120 points, respectively. Stocks tanked to…
articles.body:
Stocks rallied on Wednesday morning, after Democrats snatched back control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections .

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up by 1,104 points nearly 30 minutes after the opening bell. The Nasdaq composite and S&P 500 were up by more than 500 and 120 points, respectively.

Stocks tanked to close out last week, as investors’ concerns over tech companies’ mounting debt amid the AI build-out spurred a sell-off.

Democrats charged to victory on Tuesday, flipping the Senate and House in resounding fashion. Decision Desk HQ has called 241 House seats for Democrats and 149 for Republicans, along with 54 Senate seats for Democrats and 44 for Republicans.

Democrats across the country campaigned on cost-of-living issues, capitalizing on Americans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and persistent inflation under President Trump.

Prices at the pump have risen during the Iran war , giving Democrats an opening to flip Senate seats in traditionally ruby-red states such as Iowa, Kansas and Texas .

History shows the S&P 500 typically rises after the midterms. After midterm elections from 1982 to 2022, the index was up by an average of 0.5 percent a day later, according to a CNBC analysis .

A week and a month after those elections, the S&P 500 was respectively up by 1 percent and 1.5 percent, per CNBC.

Democrats also flipped the House in 2018, during Trump’s first term. That year, the S&P 500 was up 2.1 percent a day after the midterms, but down 1.2 percent and 2.2 percent a week and month later, respectively, according to CNBC.

“Since 1928, the S&P 500 has posted an average return of +1.0% in November … gains were recorded 62% of the time … best November +12.0% and worst November -13.4%,” Liz Ann Sonders, the chief investment strategist at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, wrote Wednesday on the social platform X.

articles.title: Why the stock market is unexpectedly rallying in the wake of the Democratic blue wave
articles.summary: Here's why stocks are doing something very different post-election from what many thought they would.
articles.body:
Call it a contrarian move. It has been a riveting 12 hours or so in the markets as investors slice and dice the midterm election outcomes.

Initially, stocks got hammered as the results trickled in. The thinking was that Democrats are less pro-business than Republicans, and since they will control the House and the Senate, there goes the corporate profit miracle that has driven the markets over the past two years.

But something very interesting has emerged after that initial knee-jerk reaction. Stocks are rallying on Wednesday — big-time!

Here are three reasons I think we're seeing this play out.

First, the midterm election results threaten to significantly disrupt AI data center expansion as voter backlash over soaring utility bills, grid instability, and water usage drive a sharp political pivot toward tighter regulatory oversight. That is being viewed as a positive for hyperscalers such as Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) in that they will be forced to pull back on spending, which would boost free cash flow.

Free cash flow declines have been at the heart of the latest AI stock sell-off, so if cash flow outlooks brighten up at the biggest companies driving the market, all the better.

Second, with the elections over, the cloud of uncertainty that had begun to seep into markets in recent weeks has been lifted. Now investors can better place their chips where they see fit.

As the team at the Stocktrader's Almanac pointed out, six months after the past 19 midterm elections, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has been higher 100% of the time, with an average gain of 14.18% .

Third, there is this callout by Goldman Sachs strategist Jan Hatzius today that also gets to the heart of this day-after rally.

Hatzius wrote: "The larger-than-expected majorities could give them slightly greater leverage in negotiations with the White House, but will also dilute the influence of small factions within the Democratic caucus. We expect Democrats to use fiscal deadlines to seek to limit the war with Iran, roll back selected tariffs, and reverse spending cuts enacted last year."

I read that as a pro-corporate bottom line.

articles.title: Reform the NAIC, don’t replace it with another Washington bureaucracy
articles.summary: Amid rising insurance costs, experts suggest reforming the National Association of Insurance Commissioners to improve accountability while maintaining state-level regulatory authority.
articles.body:
An Oct. 20 report on insurance affordability found that the average American’s homeowners insurance premiums now exceed average property-tax bills in two-thirds of U.S. counties. Inflation-adjusted premiums have risen a whopping 45 percent over the past decade.

For families already struggling with the increasingly expensive everyday cost of living, this is another burden they can hardly afford.

The growing insurance affordability crisis raises important questions about oversight of an industry on which Americans depend to protect their homes, businesses, livelihoods and well-being.

One institution especially deserving of scrutiny is the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC). Founded in 1871, the NAIC is a nonprofit organization governed by insurance regulators from all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and five U.S. territories. It helps states coordinate insurance oversight, develop model laws, establish financial solvency standards, and share regulatory information.

The NAIC provides considerable value, but the organization has transparency and accountability problems that should concern anyone who believes regulatory authority must ultimately answer to the public. Its accreditation process also places substantial pressure on states to adopt particular model laws and standards, even though the organization itself is not directly accountable to voters.

An Aug. 28 Wall Street Journal column from the Southwest Public Policy Institute highlighted the NAIC’s opaque accreditation process, limited financial disclosures, and dependence on revenue from the insurance industry — the very industry whose standards it writes.

According to the U.S. Government Accountability Office, the organization generated $161.4 million in revenue in 2024, approximately 94 percent from industry-related sources. Despite its nonprofit status, it has been exempt from filing IRS Form 990 since 1955 , so financial details like executive compensation are not publicly disclosed.

The impetus for creating this cooperative, nonprofit structure: In 1944, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in U.S. v. North-Eastern Underwriters Association that federal anti-trust laws applied to the insurance; thus, under the auspices of the Commerce Clause , Congress would set the industry’s regulations. In response, Congress passed the 1945 McCarran-Ferguson Act , which assigned back to the states the primary authority for regulating the industry. Ever since then, there has been tension between policymakers who want to centralize the regulatory regime and those who seek to preserve the states’ authority.

Clearly, there is room for reform. That said, policymakers should not view the need for reform as a call to usurp the states’ authority. Replacing state-based regulation with a centralized federal system would create additional problems rather than solve existing ones.

Insurance markets are fundamentally different across America. For example, from hurricanes to tornadoes to floods to earthquakes and wildfires, Americans require different insurance products, pricing considerations, mitigation strategies, and regulatory responses from one state to another.

A Washington-centered system could struggle to accommodate state-by-state differences. State regulators are closer to factors that shape their insurance markets. Federalism allows states to respond to local circumstances while learning from one another.

The NAIC makes effective cooperation possible. Its accreditation program promotes financial oversight and enables regulators to rely on examinations conducted by other states, reducing unnecessary duplication and expense.

A Government Accountability Office review acknowledged these benefits. Nevertheless, the review identified transparency issues that warrant attention.

Unfortunately, concerns about the NAIC have become an argument for expanding federal regulatory authority. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has questioned the organization’s oversight of insurers and private-equity investments. Such scrutiny can serve a legitimate purpose, but shortcomings in state coordination do not automatically mean that federal control would produce better results.

Rather than pursuing a federal approach, policymakers should examine reforms that strengthen accountability while preserving state authority.

Michigan offers a practical example. Under Section 500.478 of the Michigan Insurance Code , the state requires annual NAIC disclosures to state insurance officials and legislative committees, including executive compensation, accreditation requirements, and information about public access to deliberations. Other states could adopt comparable requirements.

Additional reforms should include greater transparency in accreditation proceedings, stronger conflict-of-interest safeguards, legislative oversight of model standards, and reconsideration of the NAIC’s Form 990 exemption.

Americans need affordable, reliable insurance and regulators who understand their communities. They also deserve transparency from organizations shaping the rules governing their coverage. Reforming the NAIC can advance both objectives without creating another layer of federal bureaucracy .

Kent Kaiser, Ph.D., is secretary/treasurer of the Domestic Policy Caucus .

articles.title: US markets rise as Democrats sweep midterm elections
articles.summary: Nasdaq, Dow, and S&P 500 open higher after Democrats take control and Trump accepts results.
articles.body:
US markets are trending upwards after Democrats swept the midterm elections , taking control of both the House and Senate on Tuesday.

The Nasdaq opened on Wednesday up 1 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 1.8 percent and the S&P 500 up 1.1 percent as markets opened at 9:30am ET (14:30GMT).

Retailers that rely on imports, such as Walmart and Target, are up 1.3 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively, amid possible changes in tariff policy.

Health insurance provider UnitedHealthcare is down 2.9 percent, while CVS Health is down 12 percent. However, Cigna went up 1.6 percent.

Investor sentiment was also buoyed by United States President Donald Trump’s social media post saying he would accept the results, easing political uncertainty and pressure on markets.

For companies involved in the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, the outlook is different as the Democrats have been more critical of the sector.

Oracle and Nvidia both opened the day lower, although Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is on the upswing, up 3.5 percent at the opening bell.

“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Dan Ives, managing partner of Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Wednesday.

“We estimate 10% of datacenters will not happen now,” Ives added in a post on X.

Democrats performed well in states where the AI buildout is pronounced, including Ohio, where Sherrod Brown flipped the Senate seat; Texas, where Democrats took a Senate seat with James Talarico; and the governor’s race, which Gina Hinojosa won, also flipping the seat.

Oil prices are also on the decline. The global benchmark Brent crude oil futures are down $3.20, or 3.09 percent, to $100.40 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude is down $3.01, or 3.13 percent, to $93.08.

While oil prices are reacting to the midterm results, investors are also watching to see whether the war with Iran and the one between Russia and Ukraine will end amid reports of talks, following the previous session, which saw oil prices hit their lowest levels in four weeks.

articles.title: AI's circular financing is a 'feature,' not a bug, Wall Street's elite bond committee tells Treasury
articles.summary: Treasury's top bond advisers see no crowding out from AI debt yet, even as lenders charge Oracle, CoreWeave and Amazon a lot more.
articles.body:
The cost of insuring AI borrowers' debt has jumped as much as 80% since August.

The government's top bond advisers say the money sloshing around the AI boom is built that way on purpose, and that it's mostly fine — at least for now.

The Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee , a panel of big-bank and investor executives that advises Treasury on how the US borrows, made AI debt one of its two research topics this quarter. Its presentation , out Wednesday, sums up the view in one slide title: "Circular Financing is a feature."

That's the loop of chipmakers, cloud companies and their biggest customers funding one another. The committee's bet is that the hardware outlasts some of its buyers. "While some individual compute operators might not remain viable, the physical infrastructure will continue to find demand," the presentation said.

The bill is enormous. Tech's capital spending is headed for $1 trillion this year and $1.7 trillion in 2027, by the committee's count, far more than those businesses bring in. That leaves a hole of more than $600 billion next year, and about $735 billion of new tech debt to help fill it.

"The face of AI financing has just changed," Defiance ETFs CEO Sylvia Jablonski told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday. "It used to come from the balance sheet. And it can't do that anymore."

The committee's fine print carries a warning: "The strength of the overall cohort should not obscure the vulnerabilities of individual borrowers."

Lenders seem to agree. Insuring Amazon's ( AMZN ) debt costs nearly 80% more than in early August, as its cash burn hits a record . Oracle ( ORCL ) and CoreWeave ( CRWV ) are up about 50%, against roughly 20% to 25% for the broader bond market.

Oracle's insurance now costs more than at any point in the 2008 financial crisis, after it borrowed another $10 billion . CoreWeave's price implies about a 60% chance of default within five years, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

Washington isn't feeling the squeeze yet. "Treasury auction results show no evidence that 2026 technology-related issuance has crowded out long-end Treasury demand," the committee told Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

But the two are fishing in the same pond. Treasury is borrowing short-term, so insurers and pensions hunting for long-term bonds are buying corporate debt. "When the government issues short and companies issue long, the investors who need duration most will go where the duration is," Apollo chief economist Torsten Sløk wrote last week. (Disclosure: Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management.)

articles.title: Do you use AI agents to run your daily life? We want to hear about it
articles.summary: Tech giants are betting that AI agents will play a key role in how people get things done in the future – from shopping for groceries to returning packages and planning vacations.
articles.body: Tech giants are betting that AI agents will play a key role in how people get things done in the future – from shopping for groceries to returning packages and planning vacations. OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic have made major pushes in this direction with the launch of agents like Dots, Muse and Claude Duet in recent weeks. Meta’s Muse amassed 10 million downloads in the United States in its first 40 days, making it one of the few apps to achieve that milestone according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Meta claims Muse can do things like build a shopping cart based on a recipe on Instagram, create workout plans and plan family trivia nights. CNN wants to understand how people actually use AI in their daily lives. Do you rely on ChatGPT or Muse to manage your budgets, update your calendar and keep up with emails and social plans? If so, we want to hear from you. What do you like and dislike about your AI agent? How well do you feel like your AI agent knows you? And are you aware of how much information your AI agent remembers about you? These are the kinds of questions we’d like to discuss. articles.title: Stock market today: Dow rallies 1,300 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq gain after Democrats win control of Congress
articles.summary: Markets priced in a divided government and assessed what a Democratic sweep of midterm elections means for key industries.
articles.body: US stocks jumped on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in a seismic midterm election, paving the way for a divided government.The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose 2.5%, or around 1,300 points, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) climbed 1.5%. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) traded up by 1.6% as Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT) stocks touched record highs.Markets swiftly repriced a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate — and the potential for ballot measures and newly elected officials to restrict data center construction. Chip stocks, including Nvidia (NVDA) and Micron (MU), fell more than 1%. Meanwhile, other parts of the tech sector offset some of those losses with Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT) each hitting all-time highs.Investors will also be watching for policy actions on housing and pharmaceuticals in the aftermath of the election.As Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre pointed out on Tuesday, midterm elections have a history of shaping stock performance in the near term but don't tend to move markets much over the long term.On the economic front, ISM and S&P data showed that US services activity expanded at a slower pace in October as businesses continued to grapple with elevated costs. Private-sector hiring, meanwhile, continued to show strength in October as an ADP report indicated “pretty solid job growth.”Earnings continue to roll in. AMD (AMD) posted a Q3 earnings beat, while McDonald's (MCD) grappled with slowing same-store sales growth. Duolingo (DUOL) stock soared over 30% on strong user growth.
